subject: maths
title: Volume and surface area of prisms

scenes.heading: Volume and surface area of prisms
scenes.sub: What fits inside, and what covers the outside
scenes.say: How much water fits in a trough? How much cardboard makes a box? One is volume, the other is surface area. Let's learn both for every kind of prism.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Every slice of a loaf is the same shape; stack them to make the loaf
scenes.science: Volume of a prism = area of one cross-section × length
scenes.breaks: Real bread slices vary a little; a prism's cross-section is exactly the same all the way along.
scenes.say: Think of a loaf of sliced bread. Every slice is the same shape, and stacking the slices makes the loaf. A prism is the same. Its cross-section is the same all the way along, so its volume is the area of one slice times the length.

scenes.heading: Volume of any prism
scenes.say: So the volume of any prism is capital A, the area of the cross-section, times l, the length.

scenes.heading: A triangular prism
scenes.say: First the prism is drawn, then its shaded triangle cross-section. The triangle's shorter sides, fifteen and eight, meet at the right angle, so its area is half of fifteen times eight, sixty. The prism is ten centimetres long, so the volume is six hundred cubic centimetres.
scenes.caption: The triangle's area is ½ × 15 × 8 = 60 cm². The prism is 10 cm long, so V = 600 cm³.

scenes.heading: Surface area from a net
scenes.say: Surface area is the total area of every face. Unfold a five by four by three box into its net. The faces come in pairs: twenty, fifteen and twelve square centimetres. Add one of each and double: ninety-four square centimetres.
scenes.caption: Unfold a 5 × 4 × 3 box. Faces come in pairs: 20, 15 and 12 cm². SA = 2(20 + 15 + 12) = 94 cm².

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: A trough has a trapezium cross-section 80 cm and 50 cm across, 30 cm deep, and is 200 cm long. How many litres?
scenes.say: A trough has a trapezium cross-section. Half of eighty plus fifty, times thirty, is one thousand nine hundred and fifty square centimetres. Times the length, two hundred, gives three hundred and ninety thousand cubic centimetres. A thousand cubic centimetres is one litre, so it holds three hundred and ninety litres.
scenes.caption: Cross-section ½ × (80 + 50) × 30 = 1950 cm². Times 200 gives 390 000 cm³. 1000 cm³ = 1 L, so it holds 390 L.

scenes.heading: Volume or surface area?

right.title: Surface area
points: Add every face of the net

scenes.say: Volume fills and is measured in cubic units, or millilitres and litres. Surface area covers the outside and is measured in square units. Cubed fills, squared covers.

points: SA = total area of all faces
Check for missing or extra faces
scenes.say: Quick recap. Volume is the cross-section area times the length. Surface area adds every face. One cubic centimetre is one millilitre, and one cubic metre is a thousand litres. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: Quick recap. Volume = cross-section area × length. Surface area adds every face. 1 cm³ = 1 mL, and 1 m³ = 1000 L. Now try the practice questions!
